opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd frame it a bit more carefully. I don't object to commitments in general. I object to commitments that lock in specific practices before we understand the problem well enough to know whether those practices are the right ones.

Our understanding of how to make AI systems safe is changing really quickly. If you'd asked me three or four years ago what the most important safety techniques would be, I'd have given you an answer that looks somewhat wrong in hindsight. Some things I was excited about turned out less useful than I hoped, and some things I barely thought about now seem quite central. Suppose a company had written that earlier picture into a binding commitment: "We will always do X before deploying a model at capability level Y." There's a good chance X is no longer the best use of the safety team's limited time, and maybe it was never measuring what we cared about.

So I see a couple of failure modes. The first is that you spend effort on compliance rather than on safety. People end up doing the thing because it's on the checklist, even when everyone involved agrees it isn't the most valuable thing to do right now. Safety researchers' time is scarce, and that's a real cost.

The second, and probably more worrying, is what happens when a commitment becomes clearly unworkable. Then the company either breaks it, which erodes trust in all its commitments, including the good ones, or it quietly reinterprets it, which is arguably worse because it teaches everyone that commitments are mostly PR. Neither outcome builds the kind of credibility you want for the moments when it really matters.

What I'd prefer is commitments to process and outcomes rather than to specific techniques. Something like: "We will assess these categories of risk before deployment, we'll publish what we did and why, and we'll explain our reasoning when we change approach." That keeps accountability, because outsiders can see what you're doing and criticize it. But it leaves room to update as the science improves, which I think it has to do for a while yet.

To be clear, I understand why people want firm commitments. There are real incentive problems, competitive pressure, and reasons not to simply trust companies to do the right thing. I take that seriously. I just think rigid, technique-level commitments are a fairly blunt tool for that problem, and they can backfire in ways that make things less safe rather than more.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I don't object to commitments as such. I think commitments can be really valuable. What I'm sceptical of is a particular flavour of commitment, where a company says, "We will always do X," where X is some very specific technical practice, like "We will always run this particular evaluation suite before deployment," or "We will always use this specific alignment technique." And the reason I'm sceptical is that the state of the art in alignment and safety is changing incredibly fast. If you'd asked me three or four years ago what the right safety practices were, I would have given you an answer that I now think is substantially wrong, or at least substantially incomplete. And I expect that to keep happening.

So when you make a fixed commitment about practices, you're essentially freezing your best guess at a particular point in time. And then one of two things happens. Either you actually stick to it, in which case you may end up doing something that no longer makes sense given what you've learned — maybe you're spending a lot of effort on an evaluation that turned out to not be very informative, while the thing that actually matters now isn't covered at all. Or, more realistically, people find that the commitment doesn't make sense anymore, and so they start finding ways to reinterpret it or quietly deprioritise it. And that second outcome is in some ways worse, because now you've eroded trust in commitments generally. People look at that and say, "Well, the company said they'd do this and they didn't," and it's hard to explain that actually the reason was a good one.

I think the thing I'd much rather see is commitments at the level of goals and processes rather than specific techniques. So something like: "Before we deploy a model, we will have a justified belief that it does not pose risks above some threshold, and here is the process by which we will form that belief, and here is how we will be transparent about it." That kind of commitment is robust to the field changing. If next year we discover a much better way of evaluating a model for a given risk, the commitment says you should adopt it, rather than saying you should keep doing the old thing.

The other point I'd make is that there's a real difference between what's appropriate for a company to commit to unilaterally versus what should be in regulation or an industry-wide standard. I actually think there's a stronger case for fixedness in those settings, because the whole point is that you want something enforceable and predictable, and you have mechanisms for updating it, even if they're slow. A single company making a very specific public commitment doesn't have those mechanisms in the same way, and it also gets you into the dynamic where the company becomes the entity deciding what safe behaviour means, which I'm not sure is where we want to end up.

So the short version is: I'm pro commitments, I'm just anti committing to the particular technical answer at a point where we don't yet know what the answer is. Commit to the goal, commit to the process, commit to being transparent, and leave room to get better at the actual practices.

astra-6.text:
My main concern is that we don’t yet know what the right safety and alignment practices are going to be. The evidence is changing, the systems are changing, and the techniques available to us are changing. If you make a very specific commitment now, you can end up locked into a practice that turns out not to be very useful.

Suppose you commit to running a particular evaluation before deploying a model. Later, you discover that the evaluation doesn’t really measure the risk you care about, and you have a better approach. Ideally, you’d switch. But now switching looks like breaking a safety promise, so there’s pressure to keep doing the thing you promised, even if it’s mostly busywork.

That doesn’t mean companies should have no accountability. I’d rather see commitments that allow practices to improve as we learn: be clear about what risks you’re trying to address, explain the evidence behind your decisions, and explain why you’re changing your approach. There’s a real tradeoff here, because flexibility can also be an excuse to weaken safeguards. But I don’t think freezing today’s best guesses is a good solution to that.

My main concern is that we don’t yet know what the right safety and alignment practices are going to be. We’re learning a lot, the systems are changing, and the risks we need to address may change too. So if you commit now to a particular procedure, you can end up locked into something that turns out not to be very useful.

Suppose you commit to running a particular evaluation before deploying a model. Later, you discover that the evaluation doesn’t really measure the thing you care about, and you have a better approach. You should switch. But now switching looks like walking back a safety commitment, even if it actually improves safety. That creates an incentive to keep doing the old thing, perhaps alongside the new thing, just to satisfy the commitment.

I’m much more sympathetic to commitments about how you’ll make decisions: that you’ll take evidence of serious risks seriously, explain your reasoning, and update your practices as you learn. I do think accountability matters. I just want that accountability to push companies toward making good safety decisions, rather than toward following a checklist we wrote before we understood the problem.
